title: Why Your Groceries Cost More Than Your Neighbour's
description: Does your ride really cost more when your battery is low? Case file #002 follows Larry (fictional) through one day: a viral battery rumour, a TV that got $100 dearer in a parking lot, and a real 2025 investigation in which hundreds of shoppers paid different prices for the same groceries at the same store, at the same moment.

characters.larry: a cheerful middle-aged man with a round face and a thin moustache, wearing a loud yellow checked sports jacket and a red fedora
characters.linda: a sharp, practical woman in her forties with a neat dark bob and cat-eye glasses, wearing a mint-green 1950s shirt dress
characters.price: a friendly retro 1950s department-store robot salesman with a polished round chrome head, a smiling speaker-grille mouth, a red bow tie, a small price-tag badge on its chest, and simple hands in white four-fingered cartoon gloves like a 1950s advertising mascot

Case file number two. Same basket, different price.
Ten fifteen a.m.
Larry orders his groceries on a delivery app. Across town, his sister Linda orders the exact same basket.

beats.text: That's not a made-up scene. In 2025, Consumer Reports and the Groundwork Collaborative had hundreds of volunteers buy the same basket, at the same store, at the same time.

doc.source: Summary · Consumer Reports & Groundwork Collaborative · Dec 2025
doc.headline: Same cart, different price
doc.body: 437 volunteers shopped identical baskets through Instacart at the same stores at the same moment. About three-quarters of the products checked were offered at different prices, by up to 23% per item.

beats.say: That's not a made-up scene. In twenty twenty-five, Consumer Reports and the Groundwork Collaborative had hundreds of volunteers buy the same basket, at the same store, at the same time.

beats.text: At one Safeway in Seattle, the cheapest basket came to 114 dollars 34. The most expensive: 123 dollars 93.

beats.say: At one Safeway in Seattle, the cheapest basket came to one hundred and fourteen dollars thirty-four. The most expensive: one hundred and twenty-three ninety-three.

beats.text: Nearly ten dollars of difference. On one ordinary grocery run. For nothing but luck.
Only eight percent of shoppers got the lowest total.
Quick game. Pause the video. Five price tags, one product. Which one is real?

visual.prompt: five blank paper price tags with red borders hanging on strings in a row in front of a single carton of eggs on a shop shelf

beats.text: Trick question. In these tests, some items carried up to five different prices at the very same moment.

inserts.caption: Piggly Wiggly, 1918 — the first self-service store

beats.text: Now look at these crackers. Shoppers were shown three different 'original' prices: five ninety-three, five ninety-nine, and six sixty-nine.

visual.prompt: a box of premium saltine crackers on a cream shop shelf with a red sale ribbon across it, the box front plain and unlettered

beats.text: And every single one of them paid the same sale price: three ninety-nine.
Same price. Different *feeling.*
The bigger the fake 'was', the better the deal felt. Economists call it anchoring.

beats.text: Instacart confirmed the findings reflected its own price tests, running at ten retailers. It called the differences negligible.

beats.text: Eleven forty-seven p.m.
Larry opens a ride app. The fare looks high. Is it the rain? The hour? Or the battery?
Suspect number one: the battery rumour. Alias: the three-percent tax. Last seen: every group chat since 2016.

visual.prompt: a single cream retro-styled smartphone standing upright, its battery icon nearly empty and glowing red, plain light grey background, studio lighting

beats.say: Suspect number one: the battery rumour. Alias: the three-percent tax. Last seen: every group chat since twenty sixteen.

beats.text: Here's what was actually said. Uber had noticed that riders with a nearly dead phone seemed more willing to accept surge pricing.

doc.headline: Uber's economist on dying phones
doc.body: Uber's head of economic research said riders whose phones were nearly out of battery seemed more willing to accept surge pricing. He also said Uber does not use battery level to set prices.
doc.highlight: more willing to accept surge pricing

beats.text: But he also said Uber does not use your battery to set the price. And nobody has shown that it does.
Verdict: not proven.
But notice what the rumour got right. Your phone knows things about you. Where you are. What you're doing. How badly you need it.

beats.text: And some apps really have changed the price because of one of those things. Exhibit A.

One thirty p.m.
To see why this matters, rewind a hundred and fifty years. For most of history, prices were personal. You walked into a shop, and you haggled.

visual.credit: Walker Evans / Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (no known restrictions)
visual.caption: General store, Moundville, Alabama, 1936 — Walker Evans

beats.text: Then shops like Wanamaker's in Philadelphia championed a radical idea.

visual.credit: Alfred S. Campbell stereograph, 1896, Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (no known restrictions)
visual.caption: Wanamaker's, Philadelphia, 1896

beats.text: One price, for everyone, written on a tag.

visual.prompt: a single old-fashioned paper price tag on a string hanging from a folded shirt in a grand 1870s department store

beats.text: The price tag was a promise. The rich man and the poor widow paid the same.
Personalised pricing quietly brings the haggling back.

visual.credit: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (no known restrictions)
visual.caption: Prices chalked outside a grocery, Savannah, 1939

beats.text: Except only *one* side knows the haggling is happening.
So who sets these prices now? Meet the machine. We'll call him Mister Price.

beats.text: In January 2025, staff at the US Federal Trade Commission published early findings from a study of companies that help sellers personalise prices.

doc.headline: Surveillance pricing
doc.body: There are a number of variables that can impact what products a consumer is shown or what prices (including promotions or discounts) a consumer might be offered. These include where the consumer is, who the consumer is, what the consumer is doing, and prior actions a consumer has taken.
doc.highlight: where the consumer is, who the consumer is, what the consumer is doing

beats.say: In January twenty twenty-five, staff at the US Federal Trade Commission published early findings from a study of companies that help sellers personalise prices.

beats.text: Here's the document itself. Page six.
The ingredients on the table: where you are, what device you use, what you browse, even how you move your mouse, and what you leave in your cart.

In defence of the accused.
Prices change all the time, sir. That's just shopping.
To be fair, he has a point. Shops have always tested prices, and a personalised offer can also mean a discount for the careful shopper.

beats.text: And Instacart said shoppers were put into test groups at random, by product and location. Not by who they are.

doc.headline: Random test groups
doc.body: Instacart said shoppers were put into test groups at random, by product and location, and not by personal or demographic data.

beats.text: Alibi: partial.

beats.text: Which brings us to the twist.
Larry thought the machine had picked on him. That it knew about the battery, the broke weekend, the bad luck.

visual.prompt: {larry} at his kitchen table frowning at his phone, a red marker question mark drawn on the wall behind him

beats.text: It didn't need to.
A test doesn't need to know who you are. It just needs enough people. Group A sees one price. Group B sees another. And the machine learns which one people will put up with.

beats.text: It tested everyone. At random. Like mice running through a supermarket.

beats.text: Instacart's own marketing material put it plainly: shoppers are not aware that they're in an experiment.

So, the verdict.
And the ten-second defence.
Before you pay, check the price somewhere else: another phone, logged out, or the store's own website.
